animals.name: Lion
animals.funFact: A lion's roar can be heard up to 5 miles (8 km) away!
animals.blurb: Lions are the only cats that live in big family groups called prides. Males grow thick manes as they get older.
animals.mapCaption: Grasslands of sub-Saharan Africa

animals.name: African Elephant
animals.funFact: An elephant's trunk has no bones and can hold up to 8 quarts (9 liters) of water!
animals.blurb: African elephants are the largest land animals on Earth. They live in close-knit herds led by an older female called the matriarch.
animals.mapCaption: Grasslands & forests across Africa

animals.name: Giant Panda

quickFacts.speed: Up to 20 mph (32 km/h) in short bursts

animals.funFact: Pandas spend up to 12 hours a day munching bamboo — about 20–40 lbs (9–18 kg) worth!
animals.blurb: Giant pandas are born pink, blind, and smaller than a stick of butter. They grow up eating almost nothing but bamboo.
animals.mapCaption: Mountain forests of central China

animals.name: Snowy Owl

quickFacts.speed: Up to 50 mph (80 km/h) in flight

animals.funFact: Unlike most owls, snowy owls are often awake and hunting in broad daylight!
animals.blurb: Snowy owls have thick feathers — even on their toes — to stay warm in the freezing Arctic. Males turn almost pure white as they age.
animals.mapCaption: Arctic tundra near the North Pole

animals.name: Bald Eagle
animals.funFact: Bald eagles build the biggest tree nests of any bird — some weigh over 1,000 lbs (450 kg)!
animals.blurb: Bald eagles aren't actually bald — their white head feathers just look that way from a distance. They were once endangered but have made an amazing comeback.
animals.mapCaption: Rivers & coastlines across North America

animals.name: Green Sea Turtle

quickFacts.speed: Up to 1.5 mph (2.4 km/h), faster in bursts

animals.funFact: Baby sea turtles hatch on the beach at night and crawl straight to the ocean by starlight!
animals.blurb: Green sea turtles can rest underwater for hours by slowing their heartbeat way down.
animals.mapCaption: Warm oceans around the world

animals.name: Veiled Chameleon

quickFacts.height: Head crest up to 2 in (5 cm) tall
quickFacts.speed: Slow mover — but its tongue strikes in a blink

animals.funFact: A chameleon's tongue can be as long as its whole body and shoots out faster than you can blink!
animals.blurb: Chameleons change color to show their mood and control their temperature, not just to hide. Each eye can look in a different direction at once!
animals.mapCaption: Mountain valleys of the Arabian Peninsula

animals.name: Poison Dart Frog
animals.funFact: Its bright colors work like a warning label built into its skin: "Don't eat me — I'm toxic!"
animals.blurb: Poison dart frogs get their toxins from the tiny insects they eat in the wild — frogs raised on other food aren't poisonous at all.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforest floors of South America

animals.name: Clownfish

quickFacts.speed: Slow — stays close to its home anemone

animals.funFact: Clownfish are immune to their anemone's sting and live safely tucked inside its stinging tentacles!
animals.blurb: Every clownfish starts life as a male — the largest fish in a group changes into a female when the group needs one. They rarely stray far from home.
animals.mapCaption: Coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific

animals.name: Great White Shark
animals.funFact: Great whites can sense a single drop of blood in 25 gallons (100 liters) of water!
animals.blurb: Great white sharks have rows of backup teeth ready to replace any that fall out. They're curious, careful hunters — not the mindless monsters in movies.
animals.mapCaption: Coastal waters in every ocean

animals.name: Giant Pacific Octopus

quickFacts.length: Up to 16 ft (5 m) arm-tip to arm-tip
quickFacts.speed: Jets away quickly in short bursts

animals.funFact: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood, and can squeeze its whole body through a hole the size of a coin!
animals.blurb: Giant Pacific octopuses are remarkably smart — they can solve puzzles, open jars, and even recognize different people.
animals.mapCaption: Cold coastal waters of the North Pacific

animals.name: Monarch Butterfly

quickFacts.speed: Up to 12 mph (19 km/h) in flight

animals.funFact: Monarchs fly up to 3,000 miles (4,800 km) to Mexico each winter — a trip no single butterfly ever finishes twice!
animals.blurb: Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, which makes the caterpillars — and the butterflies they become — taste bad to predators.
animals.mapCaption: Meadows and gardens across North America

animals.name: Emperor Scorpion
animals.funFact: Emperor scorpions glow blue-green under ultraviolet light!
animals.blurb: Despite its fearsome pincers, the emperor scorpion's sting is mild — about like a bee sting. It uses its strong claws, not venom, to catch food.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforests of West Africa

animals.name: Dairy Cow

quickFacts.speed: Up to 25 mph (40 km/h) in short bursts

animals.funFact: A dairy cow can produce around 6–7 gallons (25–30 liters) of milk every day!
animals.blurb: Cows are gentle herd animals with an amazing sense of smell — they can sniff out something up to 6 miles (10 km) away.
animals.mapCaption: Farms and pastures around the world

animals.name: Rabbit

quickFacts.habitat: Burrows in grassy fields; hutches & homes as pets
quickFacts.range: Native to Europe, now kept worldwide

animals.funFact: A rabbit's teeth never stop growing — that's why it needs to gnaw and chew constantly!
animals.blurb: Rabbits can see almost all the way around their heads without turning, which helps them watch for danger while they nibble.
animals.mapCaption: Native to Europe, now loved worldwide

animals.name: Three-Toed Sloth

quickFacts.speed: About 0.15 mph (0.24 km/h) — one of the slowest mammals alive

animals.funFact: Sloths only climb down to the ground about once a week — and algae grows right on their fur, giving them a greenish tint!
animals.blurb: Moving slowly saves so much energy that sloths only need a little food each day. They sleep up to 15 hours!
animals.mapCaption: Rainforest canopy of Central & South America

animals.name: Fennec Fox
animals.funFact: A fennec fox's giant ears — up to 6 in (15 cm) — help it hear prey underground and release body heat in the desert.
animals.blurb: The smallest fox in the world, the fennec fox has thickly furred paws that work like snowshoes for walking on hot sand.
animals.mapCaption: Sandy dunes of the Sahara Desert

animals.name: Polar Bear

quickFacts.speed: Up to 25 mph (40 km/h) on land

animals.funFact: A polar bear's skin is black under its fur, and each hair is actually clear, not white — it just reflects light to look white!
animals.blurb: Polar bears are powerful swimmers, paddling with their huge front paws across miles of open Arctic water.
animals.mapCaption: Sea ice around the Arctic Circle

animals.name: Red-Eyed Tree Frog
animals.funFact: Its bright red eyes may startle predators just long enough for it to leap to safety — scientists call this "startle coloration."
animals.blurb: Red-eyed tree frogs sleep through the day stuck to the underside of leaves, then wake up bright green and ready to hunt at night.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforests of Central America

animals.name: Axolotl
animals.funFact: Axolotls can regrow an entire lost leg, tail, or even part of their heart or brain!
animals.blurb: Unlike most amphibians, axolotls never grow up — they keep their feathery gills and stay underwater their whole lives.
animals.mapCaption: A single lake system near Mexico City

animals.name: Fire-Bellied Toad
animals.funFact: When threatened, it flips over to flash its bright red-and-black belly — a warning move called the "unken reflex"!
animals.blurb: Fire-bellied toads spend most of their time floating at the pond's surface, popping up to snap at insects that fly too close.
animals.mapCaption: Ponds and wetlands across East Asia

animals.name: Seahorse

quickFacts.length: Same as its height — it swims upright
quickFacts.speed: One of the slowest fish alive

animals.funFact: Seahorse dads carry the eggs in a special pouch and give birth to the babies themselves!
animals.blurb: Seahorses swim upright, wrap their tails around seagrass to anchor themselves, and can move each eye independently.
animals.mapCaption: Seagrass beds in warm coastal waters

animals.name: Koi
animals.funFact: Some koi have lived to be over 100 years old — they're one of the longest-living pets in the world!
animals.blurb: Koi are a colorful, patterned type of carp bred for centuries in Japan. Each one has a unique pattern, like a fingerprint.
animals.mapCaption: Native to East Asia, now kept in ponds worldwide

animals.name: Piranha
animals.funFact: Piranhas mostly travel in schools for protection from bigger predators — not to hunt in a feeding frenzy like the movies show!
animals.blurb: Despite their scary reputation, piranhas are usually shy and mainly eat other fish, insects, and even fruit that falls into the water.
animals.mapCaption: Rivers of the Amazon basin

animals.name: Hammerhead Shark
animals.funFact: Its wide, hammer-shaped head spreads its eyes far apart, giving it an almost 360-degree view of the water around it.
animals.blurb: Scientists think the hammer shape also helps this shark pin down one of its favorite meals: stingrays hiding in the sand.
animals.mapCaption: Warm coastal waters worldwide

animals.name: Whale Shark
animals.funFact: The whale shark is the biggest fish in the entire ocean — but it eats some of the smallest food: tiny plankton!
animals.blurb: Despite its giant size, the gentle whale shark has no interest in people. It simply swims along with its huge mouth open, filtering food from the water.
animals.mapCaption: Warm tropical oceans worldwide

animals.name: Nurse Shark

quickFacts.speed: Slow swimmer, rests on the seafloor

animals.funFact: Nurse sharks can pump water over their gills while lying still, so unlike most sharks, they can rest motionless on the ocean floor.
animals.blurb: By day, nurse sharks nap in piles under ledges. At night, they use whisker-like barbels near their mouth to feel for food in the sand.
animals.mapCaption: Shallow reefs of the Atlantic and Eastern Pacific

animals.name: Komodo Dragon

quickFacts.height: Stands about 20 in at the hip (50 cm)
quickFacts.speed: Up to 13 mph (20 km/h) in short bursts

animals.funFact: The world's biggest lizard, a Komodo dragon can eat up to 80% of its own body weight in a single meal!
animals.blurb: Komodo dragons have a powerful sense of smell that can detect food from miles away, and a bite that quickly weakens their prey.
animals.mapCaption: A handful of islands in Indonesia

animals.name: Bearded Dragon
animals.funFact: When it feels threatened, a bearded dragon puffs out the spiky skin under its chin to look bigger — that's how it got its name!
animals.blurb: One of the most popular pet lizards in the world, bearded dragons are known for being calm, curious, and easy to handle.
animals.mapCaption: Dry woodlands of central Australia

animals.name: Roadrunner
animals.funFact: The roadrunner would rather run than fly — it can sprint faster than most humans jog!
animals.blurb: This speedy desert bird hunts lizards, insects, and even small snakes, using its quick legs more than its short, rounded wings.
animals.mapCaption: Desert scrublands of the American Southwest

animals.name: Camel

quickFacts.speed: Up to 40 mph (65 km/h) in short bursts

animals.funFact: A camel's hump doesn't store water — it stores fat, which its body can turn into water and energy when food is scarce.
animals.blurb: Camels can drink up to 40 gallons (150 liters) of water in one go, and their thick eyelashes and closable nostrils keep desert sand out.
animals.mapCaption: Deserts of North Africa and the Middle East

animals.name: Arctic Fox
animals.funFact: An arctic fox's fur changes with the seasons — white in winter snow, brown-gray in summer tundra.
animals.blurb: Arctic foxes curl their fluffy tails around their bodies like a blanket to stay warm in temperatures colder than a freezer.
animals.mapCaption: Tundra around the Arctic Circle

animals.name: Walrus
animals.funFact: A walrus's tusks can grow up to 3 feet (1 m) long — it uses them to haul its huge body onto the ice like ice picks.
animals.blurb: Walruses use their whiskers to feel for clams buried in the dark seafloor, then slurp the shellfish right out of their shells.
animals.mapCaption: Sea ice and coasts of the Arctic Ocean

animals.name: Honeybee

quickFacts.lifespan: A few weeks (workers); up to 5 years (queen)

animals.funFact: A honeybee "dances" in a figure-eight pattern to tell the rest of the hive exactly where to find food!
animals.blurb: Honeybees pollinate about a third of the food we eat, working together in colonies of tens of thousands of bees.
animals.mapCaption: Kept in hives and found wild around the world

animals.name: Ladybug
animals.funFact: A single ladybug can eat as many as 5,000 aphids in its lifetime, making it a gardener's best friend!
animals.blurb: Those spots are more than decoration — they warn predators that ladybugs taste bitter, thanks to a yellowish fluid they release when scared.
animals.mapCaption: Gardens and fields around the world

animals.name: Dragonfly

quickFacts.lifespan: A few months as an adult

animals.funFact: A dragonfly can see almost 360 degrees at once and fly backwards, forwards, and even hover in place like a helicopter!
animals.blurb: Before becoming a flying adult, a dragonfly spends most of its life underwater as a hunting nymph, sometimes for several years.
animals.mapCaption: Ponds and wetlands around the world

animals.name: Tarantula
animals.funFact: Despite its scary looks, this tarantula's bite is milder than a bee sting — its main defense is flicking tiny irritating hairs.
animals.blurb: One of the calmest, most popular pet tarantulas in the world, it can live for decades and barely needs to eat more than once a week.
animals.mapCaption: Dry scrublands of Chile

animals.name: Garden Spider

quickFacts.speed: Sits still, waiting in its web

animals.funFact: This spider weaves a bold zigzag pattern, called a stabilimentum, right through the middle of its web.
animals.blurb: Each night, the garden spider often eats her old web and spins a fresh one before morning, recycling the silk.
animals.mapCaption: Gardens and meadows across North America

animals.name: Black Widow Spider

quickFacts.speed: Slow crawler, stays near its web

animals.funFact: Only the female black widow has the famous red hourglass marking — and she's about twice the size of the male.
animals.blurb: Black widows are shy and would rather hide than bite — they mostly stay tucked in their messy, irregular webs waiting for prey.
animals.mapCaption: Quiet, sheltered spots across North America

animals.name: Chicken
animals.funFact: Chickens can remember over 100 different faces — including other chickens and people!
animals.blurb: A mother hen starts clucking to her chicks before they even hatch, and the chicks chirp back to her from inside the egg.
animals.mapCaption: Farms and backyard coops around the world

animals.name: Ball Python
animals.funFact: When scared, a ball python curls into a tight ball with its head tucked safely in the middle — that’s how it got its name!
animals.blurb: One of the calmest, most popular pet snakes in the world, ball pythons come in hundreds of different color patterns bred by keepers.
animals.mapCaption: Grasslands of West and Central Africa

animals.name: Corn Snake
animals.funFact: Corn snakes are excellent climbers and can flatten their bodies to squeeze through tiny gaps!
animals.blurb: Named for the corn-like pattern on their bellies, corn snakes are gentle, easy to handle, and a favorite first pet snake.
animals.mapCaption: Fields and farmland of the southeastern US

animals.name: King Cobra

quickFacts.height: Can rear up 3 ft (1 m) off the ground
quickFacts.speed: Up to 12 mph (19 km/h) short bursts

animals.funFact: The king cobra is the only snake that builds a nest for its eggs, guarding them fiercely until they hatch.
animals.blurb: The world’s longest venomous snake mostly hunts other snakes, and can lift the front third of its body straight up when threatened.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforests of South and Southeast Asia

animals.name: Green Tree Python
animals.funFact: Baby green tree pythons hatch bright yellow or red and only turn green after about a year!
animals.blurb: This snake spends nearly its whole life coiled over a branch, looped in a neat pile with its head resting in the middle.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforest canopy of New Guinea and northern Australia

animals.name: Garter Snake
animals.funFact: Garter snakes are one of the few snakes that give birth to live babies instead of laying eggs — up to 80 at once!
animals.blurb: Common in backyards across North America, garter snakes are harmless and help control slugs, worms, and pests.
animals.mapCaption: Meadows and gardens across North America

animals.name: Boa Constrictor
animals.funFact: A boa constrictor doesn’t crush its prey to pieces — it squeezes just tight enough to stop the heart from beating.
animals.blurb: Boas are ambush hunters that can go weeks or months between meals, using heat-sensing pits to find warm prey in the dark.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforests and scrublands of Central and South America

animals.name: Rattlesnake
animals.funFact: A rattlesnake’s rattle is made of hollow segments — the same material as your fingernails — that click together as a warning.
animals.blurb: Rattlesnakes sense heat through pits near their nose, letting them find and strike warm-blooded prey even in total darkness.
animals.mapCaption: Deserts of the American Southwest

animals.name: Green Anaconda
animals.funFact: The green anaconda is the heaviest snake on Earth — one adult can weigh more than three grown men combined!
animals.blurb: Anacondas spend most of their time in water, where their weight barely matters and they can ambush prey while staying almost invisible.
animals.mapCaption: Swamps and slow rivers of South America

animals.name: Milk Snake
animals.funFact: Milk snakes wear the same bold red, black, and yellow bands as venomous coral snakes — a clever bluff that scares off predators!
animals.blurb: Completely harmless despite its warning colors, the milk snake copies a dangerous look to stay safe without needing venom at all.
animals.mapCaption: Forests and farmland across North and Central America

animals.name: Reticulated Python
animals.funFact: The reticulated python is the longest snake species in the world — some have measured over 20 feet (6 m) long!
animals.blurb: Despite its huge size, this python is a shy, patient ambush hunter that relies on excellent camouflage rather than chasing prey.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforests and riverbanks of Southeast Asia

animals.name: Green Iguana

quickFacts.height: Up to 2 ft including crest (0.6 m)
quickFacts.speed: Up to 21 mph (34 km/h) on land

animals.funFact: A green iguana can hold its breath underwater for up to 30 minutes and often escapes danger by dropping from trees into rivers below.
animals.blurb: Green iguanas have a third "eye" on top of their head that senses light and shadow, helping them spot predators from above.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforest canopy near water in Central and South America

animals.name: Leopard Gecko
animals.funFact: Unlike most geckos, leopard geckos have movable eyelids and can blink — and they can drop their tail to escape a predator!
animals.blurb: One of the most popular pet lizards, leopard geckos store fat in their tails and come in many different colors and spot patterns.
animals.mapCaption: Rocky deserts of South and Central Asia

animals.name: Gila Monster
animals.funFact: The Gila monster is one of the only venomous lizards in the world, and it stores fat in its tail to survive months without eating.
animals.blurb: Despite its fearsome name, this slow-moving lizard spends over 90% of its life hidden underground, rarely coming out to hunt.
animals.mapCaption: Deserts of the American Southwest

animals.name: Blue-Tongued Skink
animals.funFact: When threatened, this skink flashes its bright blue tongue to startle predators — a shocking pop of color they don’t expect!
animals.blurb: Blue-tongued skinks are calm and curious, and reptile keepers say they recognize their owners and seem to enjoy being handled.
animals.mapCaption: Woodlands and grasslands of Australia and New Guinea

animals.name: Frilled Lizard

quickFacts.speed: Up to 30 mph (48 km/h) on two legs

animals.funFact: When startled, a frilled lizard snaps open a huge neck frill, hisses, and can sprint away on just its back two legs!
animals.blurb: This lizard’s dramatic frill display is mostly a bluff — it makes the lizard look much bigger and scarier than it really is.
animals.mapCaption: Tropical woodlands of northern Australia

animals.name: Chinese Water Dragon
animals.funFact: When frightened, a water dragon dives into a stream and can stay underwater for up to 25 minutes to hide from danger.
animals.blurb: These agile lizards spend their days basking on branches over water, ready to drop straight down and swim away at any sign of trouble.
animals.mapCaption: Forest streams of Southeast Asia

animals.name: Thorny Devil
animals.funFact: A thorny devil eats nothing but ants — one lizard can eat up to 3,000 in a single day, and its spikes gather dew for it to drink!
animals.blurb: Covered head to tail in sharp spikes, this small desert lizard has a fake "head" bump on its neck to confuse predators about which end to bite.
animals.mapCaption: Sandy deserts of central Australia

animals.name: Galápagos Tortoise
animals.funFact: Galápagos tortoises can live over 150 years and go a full year without eating or drinking if they need to.
animals.blurb: The largest tortoise species in the world, these gentle giants grow so slowly they don’t reach full size until about 40 years old.
animals.mapCaption: The Galápagos Islands off South America

animals.name: Red-Eared Slider
animals.funFact: Red-eared sliders "slide" off logs into the water the instant they sense danger nearby — hence the name!
animals.blurb: One of the most popular pet turtles in the world, red-eared sliders spend hours basking in the sun to warm their cold-blooded bodies.
animals.mapCaption: Ponds and rivers of the southern United States

animals.name: Leatherback Sea Turtle
animals.funFact: The leatherback is the biggest sea turtle on Earth and can dive deeper than 4,000 feet (1,200 m) chasing jellyfish.
animals.blurb: Unlike other turtles, a leatherback’s shell is soft and rubbery instead of hard, letting it dive to incredible depths without cracking.
animals.mapCaption: Open oceans around the world

animals.name: Box Turtle
animals.funFact: A box turtle can pull its head, legs, and tail completely inside its shell and snap the hinged bottom shut like a box!
animals.blurb: Box turtles often live their whole long lives in the very same small patch of forest, rarely wandering far from home.
animals.mapCaption: Forests and meadows of the eastern United States

animals.name: Snapping Turtle
animals.funFact: A snapping turtle’s neck can shoot out almost as far as its own shell is long, striking faster than you can blink!
animals.blurb: Too big to fully hide in its small shell, this turtle relies on a powerful bite and fierce attitude to defend itself instead.
animals.mapCaption: Muddy ponds and rivers across North America

animals.name: Loggerhead Sea Turtle
animals.funFact: A loggerhead has powerful jaw muscles strong enough to crack open crabs and conch shells with ease.
animals.blurb: Named for its extra-large head, the loggerhead swims thousands of miles before returning to nest on the very beach where it hatched.
animals.mapCaption: Coastal and open oceans worldwide

animals.name: Russian Tortoise
animals.funFact: Russian tortoises are champion diggers, building deep burrows to escape both freezing winters and scorching desert heat.
animals.blurb: Small and hardy, this tortoise is one of the most popular pet tortoises thanks to its manageable size and curious personality.
animals.mapCaption: Dry steppe and desert of Central Asia

animals.name: Painted Turtle
animals.funFact: Painted turtles can survive being frozen almost solid under pond ice all winter, slowing their bodies to nearly a stop.
animals.blurb: North America’s most widespread turtle, the painted turtle gets its name from the bright red and yellow stripes on its head and legs.
animals.mapCaption: Ponds and marshes across North America

animals.name: Hawksbill Sea Turtle
animals.funFact: Hawksbills eat sea sponges that are toxic to almost every other animal, using their pointed beak to reach food in reef crevices.
animals.blurb: Named for its narrow, bird-like beak, the hawksbill helps keep coral reefs healthy by keeping sponge populations in balance.
animals.mapCaption: Coral reefs in tropical oceans worldwide

animals.name: Desert Tortoise
animals.funFact: A desert tortoise can go up to a year without drinking water, storing it in a special pouch beneath its shell.
animals.blurb: Desert tortoises dig deep burrows to escape blistering daytime heat, spending most of their lives resting safely underground.
animals.mapCaption: Deserts of the American Southwest

animals.name: Red Panda
animals.funFact: A red panda wraps its bushy tail around its body like a warm blanket while it sleeps.
animals.blurb: Despite the name, red pandas aren’t closely related to giant pandas — they’re their own unique family, and expert tree climbers.
animals.mapCaption: Mountain forests of the Himalayas

animals.name: Giraffe
animals.funFact: A giraffe’s tongue can be up to 20 inches (50 cm) long — long enough to clean its own ears!
animals.blurb: The tallest animal on Earth, a giraffe’s long neck has the same seven neck bones as a human — just much, much bigger.
animals.mapCaption: Savannas of sub-Saharan Africa

animals.name: Zebra
animals.funFact: No two zebras have the same stripe pattern — each one is as unique as a human fingerprint!
animals.blurb: Zebras live in tight family herds, and their stripes may help confuse predators and biting flies when the herd moves together.
animals.mapCaption: Grasslands of eastern and southern Africa

animals.name: Ostrich
animals.funFact: The ostrich is the fastest animal on two legs and lays the largest egg of any bird — about the size of 24 chicken eggs!
animals.blurb: Too big and heavy to fly, ostriches instead rely on powerful legs that can deliver a kick strong enough to injure a lion.
animals.mapCaption: Savannas and plains of sub-Saharan Africa

animals.name: Peacock

quickFacts.length: Up to 7.5 ft incl. tail (2.3 m)

animals.funFact: A peacock’s giant tail feathers aren’t actually its tail — they’re extra-long feathers that grow just above it!
animals.blurb: Only males grow the dazzling, eye-spotted feathers, which they fan out and shake to impress females during courtship.
animals.mapCaption: Forests and farmland of India and Sri Lanka

animals.name: Flamingo
animals.funFact: A flamingo’s pink color comes entirely from the shrimp and algae it eats — chicks are actually born gray!
animals.blurb: Flamingos often stand on one leg for hours, which may help them conserve body heat while resting in cool, shallow water.
animals.mapCaption: Shallow lagoons across Africa, Europe and Asia

animals.name: Emperor Penguin
animals.funFact: Emperor penguin dads balance the egg on their feet and huddle together through months of Antarctic winter while the moms hunt at sea.
animals.blurb: The tallest penguin species can dive deeper than 1,800 feet (550 m) and hold its breath over 20 minutes hunting for fish.
animals.mapCaption: Antarctic sea ice

animals.name: Great Horned Owl
animals.funFact: A great horned owl’s "horns" are just tufts of feathers — and its grip is strong enough to snap a rabbit’s spine instantly.
animals.blurb: This powerful owl can turn its head almost all the way around and hunts silently thanks to special feathers that muffle sound.
animals.mapCaption: Forests and deserts across the Americas

animals.name: Toucan
animals.funFact: A toucan’s giant, colorful beak is mostly hollow and lightweight, and it helps the bird release body heat to stay cool.
animals.blurb: Toucans use their long beak to reach fruit at the tips of thin branches too weak to hold the rest of their body.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforest canopy of South America

animals.name: American Bullfrog
animals.funFact: A bullfrog’s deep "jug-o-rum" call can be heard from over a quarter mile away on a quiet night.
animals.blurb: North America’s largest frog will eat almost anything that fits in its mouth — insects, fish, mice, and even other frogs.
animals.mapCaption: Ponds and marshes of eastern North America

animals.name: Hellbender Salamander
animals.funFact: The hellbender breathes almost entirely through its wrinkly skin, which soaks up oxygen straight from flowing water.
animals.blurb: North America’s largest salamander hides under flat rocks in clean, fast rivers, and its presence signals healthy water.
animals.mapCaption: Cold rivers of the eastern United States

animals.name: Tomato Frog
animals.funFact: When grabbed, a tomato frog puffs up and oozes a sticky, irritating goo that makes it hard for a predator to hold on.
animals.blurb: Named for its bright red-orange color, the tomato frog uses its bold look as a warning that it doesn’t taste very good.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforests and marshes of Madagascar

animals.name: Surinam Toad
animals.funFact: A mother Surinam toad carries her eggs embedded in the skin on her own back until fully-formed baby toads pop out!
animals.blurb: Completely flat with tiny eyes, this toad looks like a dead leaf drifting underwater — perfect camouflage for ambushing prey.
animals.mapCaption: Slow rivers and swamps of South America

animals.name: Chinese Giant Salamander
animals.funFact: The world’s largest amphibian can grow nearly six feet long — as long as a grown adult is tall!
animals.blurb: This giant salamander has poor eyesight and instead senses tiny vibrations in the water to find fish in total darkness.
animals.mapCaption: Cold mountain streams of central China

animals.name: Glass Frog
animals.funFact: A glass frog’s belly skin is see-through — you can actually watch its tiny heart beating and organs working!
animals.blurb: These tiny frogs sit on leaves above rushing streams, using their transparent underside as camouflage against the light.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforest streams of Central and South America

animals.name: Betta Fish
animals.funFact: Male betta fish are also called "Siamese fighting fish" because two males will flare their fins and fight if placed together.
animals.blurb: Bettas can gulp air at the water’s surface using a special organ, letting them survive in shallow, low-oxygen puddles.
animals.mapCaption: Rice paddies and ponds of Thailand and Southeast Asia

animals.name: Goldfish
animals.funFact: A goldfish’s memory lasts far longer than three seconds — they can remember and learn tricks for months!
animals.blurb: One of the very first fish ever kept as pets, goldfish were bred from wild carp in China over a thousand years ago.
animals.mapCaption: Native to East Asia, kept in ponds worldwide

animals.name: Angelfish
animals.funFact: Angelfish pair up and both parents fan their eggs with their fins to keep them clean and full of oxygen.
animals.blurb: With tall, triangular fins and a flat body, angelfish glide gracefully between plants and roots in slow-moving Amazon waters.
animals.mapCaption: Slow rivers of the Amazon basin

animals.name: Pufferfish
animals.funFact: A pufferfish gulps water to blow its body up to several times its normal size in seconds, making it too big to swallow.
animals.blurb: Many pufferfish also carry a toxin far deadlier than cyanide, making them one of the most poisonous animals a predator could bite.
animals.mapCaption: Coral reefs and coastal waters worldwide

animals.name: Lionfish
animals.funFact: A lionfish’s striped fins hide up to 18 venomous spines — a painful defense used only when it feels threatened.
animals.blurb: Lionfish corner small fish using their huge fanned fins like a net, then swallow prey whole in a single quick gulp.
animals.mapCaption: Coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific

animals.name: Anglerfish
animals.funFact: A deep-sea anglerfish dangles a glowing lure right above its mouth to attract curious prey out of the pitch-black water.
animals.blurb: Living over half a mile down where sunlight never reaches, anglerfish make their own light through a glowing bacteria-filled lure.
animals.mapCaption: Deep, dark oceans around the world

animals.name: Tiger Shark
animals.funFact: Tiger sharks will eat almost anything — scientists have found license plates, tires, and even armor in their stomachs!
animals.blurb: Named for the dark stripes on young sharks that fade with age, tiger sharks are curious hunters that roam huge stretches of ocean.
animals.mapCaption: Tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide

animals.name: Bull Shark
animals.funFact: Bull sharks can survive in both salt and fresh water, and have been found hundreds of miles up rivers, even in lakes.
animals.blurb: Thick-bodied and unusually adaptable, bull sharks tolerate low-salt water better than almost any other shark species.
animals.mapCaption: Warm coastal waters and rivers worldwide

animals.name: Mako Shark
animals.funFact: The mako is the fastest shark in the ocean and can even leap 20 feet (6 m) out of the water!
animals.blurb: Built like a torpedo with a warm-blooded advantage over most fish, the mako can outswim nearly everything else in the sea.
animals.mapCaption: Open oceans in temperate and tropical waters

animals.name: Lemon Shark
animals.funFact: Young lemon sharks return to the same shallow nursery bay where they were born, sometimes for several years.
animals.blurb: Named for its pale yellow-brown skin, the lemon shark is a favorite for researchers since it tolerates study in shallow water well.
animals.mapCaption: Shallow coastal reefs of the Atlantic and Eastern Pacific

animals.name: Goblin Shark
animals.funFact: A goblin shark’s jaw can shoot forward out of its mouth to snatch prey, then snap back like a slingshot!
animals.blurb: Rarely seen alive, this deep-sea shark has a long, flat snout packed with sensors that detect prey in complete darkness.
animals.mapCaption: Deep ocean slopes around the world

animals.name: Basking Shark
animals.funFact: The basking shark is the second-largest fish in the world, but it only eats tiny plankton, filtering thousands of gallons of water an hour.
animals.blurb: Often seen "basking" near the surface with its huge mouth wide open, this gentle giant poses no threat to swimmers at all.
animals.mapCaption: Temperate oceans worldwide

animals.name: Praying Mantis
animals.funFact: A praying mantis can turn its head almost 180 degrees to look over its own shoulder — no other insect can do that!
animals.blurb: Named for its folded front legs that look like praying hands, the mantis uses them to snatch prey in a lightning-fast strike.
animals.mapCaption: Gardens and fields around the world

animals.name: Firefly
animals.funFact: A firefly makes its glow through a chemical reaction that produces almost no heat at all — the most efficient light known!
animals.blurb: Each firefly species flashes its own special pattern of light, like a secret code, to find and recognize the right mate in the dark.
animals.mapCaption: Meadows and wetlands around the world

animals.name: Grasshopper
animals.funFact: A grasshopper’s powerful back legs can launch it 20 times its own body length in a single jump!
animals.blurb: Grasshoppers "sing" by rubbing their back legs against their wings, a sound called stridulation used to attract mates.
animals.mapCaption: Meadows and fields around the world

animals.name: Leafcutter Ant

quickFacts.lifespan: Workers: weeks; queens: up to 20 years

animals.funFact: A single leafcutter ant colony can strip an entire tree of leaves in just one day, using the leaves to grow fungus for food.
animals.blurb: An ant can carry up to 50 times its own body weight — like a human lifting a car — using powerful jaws and a strong grip.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforest floors of Central and South America

animals.name: Stick Insect

quickFacts.length: Up to 14 in with legs extended (36 cm)

animals.funFact: One of the longest insects in the world, the stick insect sways gently to mimic a twig blowing in the wind.
animals.blurb: Stick insects rely almost entirely on looking exactly like a twig or leaf to avoid being noticed and eaten by hungry birds.
animals.mapCaption: Rainforest trees of Southeast Asia

animals.name: Luna Moth
animals.funFact: Adult luna moths have no mouth at all — they live for about a week using only energy stored from their caterpillar stage.
animals.blurb: With pale green wings and long trailing tails, luna moths flutter through forests at night, guided mostly by moonlight and scent.
animals.mapCaption: Forests of eastern North America

animals.name: Camel Spider

quickFacts.length: Up to 6 in leg span (15 cm)

animals.funFact: Despite scary rumors, camel spiders aren’t venomous and aren’t even true spiders — they’re a separate group called solifuges.
animals.blurb: This fast desert hunter uses huge jaws to chase down insects and small lizards, relying on speed rather than venom.
animals.mapCaption: Sandy deserts of the Middle East and North Africa

animals.name: Whip Scorpion
animals.funFact: When threatened, a whip scorpion sprays a vinegar-smelling acid from its tail — earning it the nickname "vinegaroon"!
animals.blurb: Despite its name and pincers, the whip scorpion has no venomous stinger — its whip-like tail is used only for defense.
animals.mapCaption: Deserts and forest floors of the southern US and Mexico

animals.name: Huntsman Spider

quickFacts.length: Up to 12 in leg span (30 cm)

animals.funFact: A huntsman spider can run sideways almost as fast as a person walks, using a crab-like scuttle to chase prey.
animals.blurb: One of the largest spiders by leg span, the huntsman hunts by chasing prey down instead of spinning a web to trap it.
animals.mapCaption: Forests and homes across tropical regions

animals.name: Wolf Spider
animals.funFact: A mother wolf spider carries her babies riding on her back until they’re old enough to survive on their own.
animals.blurb: Unlike most spiders, wolf spiders don’t spin webs to catch food — they chase down and pounce on prey like tiny, eight-legged wolves.
animals.mapCaption: Grasslands and gardens around the world

animals.name: Daddy Long Legs
animals.funFact: Despite the legend, daddy long legs aren’t even spiders, and scientists have found they have no venom at all.
animals.blurb: Unlike true spiders, a harvestman’s body is a single rounded blob with one pair of eyes, held up on impossibly long, thin legs.
animals.mapCaption: Gardens and forests around the world

animals.name: Deathstalker Scorpion
animals.funFact: The deathstalker’s powerful venom is being studied by scientists to help treat cancer and diabetes.
animals.blurb: This pale yellow scorpion hides under rocks by day, using its venom at night to quickly subdue insects and small prey.
animals.mapCaption: Rocky deserts of North Africa and the Middle East

animals.name: Pig
animals.funFact: Pigs are one of the smartest farm animals — smarter than dogs by some tests — and can learn tricks and solve simple puzzles.
animals.blurb: Pigs love to roll in mud not because they’re messy, but because they can’t sweat and mud helps keep them cool.
animals.mapCaption: Farms and pastures around the world

animals.name: Sheep
animals.funFact: A sheep’s wool never stops growing — without regular shearing, it would keep getting thicker every year.
animals.blurb: Sheep have excellent peripheral vision, able to see almost all the way around their body without turning their head.
animals.mapCaption: Farms and hillsides around the world

animals.name: Goat
animals.funFact: Goats have rectangular pupils that give them an almost 340-degree field of vision to watch for predators.
animals.blurb: Goats are excellent climbers that can scale steep cliffs and even trees in search of leaves, using their nimble hooves.
animals.mapCaption: Farms and hillsides around the world

animals.name: Horse
animals.funFact: Horses can sleep both lying down and standing up, thanks to a special leg-locking mechanism that keeps them from falling.
animals.blurb: Horses can recognize human facial expressions and even remember people they haven’t seen in years.
animals.mapCaption: Farms and pastures around the world

animals.name: Duck
animals.funFact: A duck’s feathers are coated in natural oil that keeps water from soaking through — that’s why water rolls right off its back.
animals.blurb: Ducklings imprint on the first moving thing they see after hatching, usually their mother, and follow it everywhere.
animals.mapCaption: Ponds, farms and wetlands around the world

animals.name: Turkey
animals.funFact: Wild turkeys can fly fast for short bursts and see nearly 270 degrees around them without turning their head.
animals.blurb: A male turkey’s head can change color from red to blue in seconds depending on its mood, and its fanned tail impresses mates.
animals.mapCaption: Farms and forest edges of North America

animals.name: Beluga Whale
animals.funFact: Belugas are nicknamed "sea canaries" because of the wide range of clicks, whistles, and squeals they use to talk to each other.
animals.blurb: Unlike most whales, a beluga can turn its head from side to side, and its round forehead can change shape as it makes sounds.
animals.mapCaption: Arctic and sub-Arctic coastal waters

animals.name: Narwhal

quickFacts.length: 13–16 ft body, tusk up to 10 ft (4–5 m + 3 m tusk)

animals.funFact: A narwhal’s long spiral tusk is actually a giant tooth packed with millions of nerve endings.
animals.blurb: Often called the "unicorn of the sea," male narwhals use their tusks to spar with rivals and sense their surroundings.
animals.mapCaption: Sea ice and deep waters of the Arctic Ocean

animals.name: Musk Ox
animals.funFact: When threatened, a herd of musk oxen forms a tight circle with the calves safely hidden in the middle, horns facing outward.
animals.blurb: Musk oxen grow an extremely thick undercoat called qiviut, one of the warmest and softest wools in the world, to survive Arctic winters.
animals.mapCaption: Arctic tundra of North America and Greenland

animals.name: Arctic Hare
animals.funFact: An Arctic hare can hop upright on its two back legs like a kangaroo to see over snow and spot predators.
animals.blurb: Its thick white winter coat provides such good camouflage against the snow that Arctic hares are nearly invisible until they move.
animals.mapCaption: Arctic tundra of North America and Greenland

animals.name: Puffin
animals.funFact: A puffin can carry more than 10 small fish at once in its beak, thanks to backward-pointing spines on its tongue.
animals.blurb: Puffins spend most of the year alone at sea, only coming to land in big, noisy colonies to nest on sea cliffs each summer.
animals.mapCaption: Sea cliffs of the North Atlantic

animals.name: Reindeer

quickFacts.range: Arctic regions of North America, Europe & Asia

animals.funFact: Reindeer are the only deer species where both males and females grow antlers, and they can see ultraviolet light to spot food and predators in the snow.
animals.blurb: Reindeer herds migrate over 3,000 miles a year, the longest land migration of any mammal on Earth, following food across the frozen tundra.
animals.mapCaption: Tundra and forests across the Arctic

animals.name: American Alligator

quickFacts.speed: Up to 20 mph (32 km/h) in short bursts

animals.funFact: An American alligator can go through more than 2,000 teeth in its lifetime — new ones just grow in to replace worn-out ones!
animals.blurb: Once endangered, American alligators made one of the greatest comebacks in conservation history and now thrive in swamps across the South.
animals.mapCaption: Swamps and rivers of the southeastern United States

animals.name: Saltwater Crocodile

quickFacts.speed: Up to 18 mph (29 km/h) in water

animals.funFact: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile on Earth — and it can swim far out into the open ocean!
animals.blurb: Saltwater crocodiles are powerful ambush hunters that can hold perfectly still for hours before exploding into a lightning-fast strike.
animals.mapCaption: Coastal waters of northern Australia and Southeast Asia

animals.name: Nile Crocodile

quickFacts.speed: Up to 22 mph (35 km/h) in short bursts

animals.funFact: A Nile crocodile's bite is one of the strongest of any animal alive — but the muscles that open its jaw are so weak a hand can hold them shut.
animals.blurb: Nile crocodiles patiently wait at river crossings for months, ambushing herds of migrating animals as they cross the water.
animals.mapCaption: Rivers and lakes across sub-Saharan Africa

animals.name: Gharial
animals.funFact: A gharial's long, narrow snout is lined with over 100 needle-thin teeth perfect for snatching slippery fish.
animals.blurb: Male gharials grow a strange bulb on the tip of their snout, used to make buzzing noises and blow bubbles to attract mates.
animals.mapCaption: Fast-flowing rivers of northern India and Nepal

animals.name: American Crocodile

quickFacts.speed: Up to 20 mph (32 km/h) in short bursts

animals.funFact: Unlike alligators, American crocodiles have a narrower snout and a visible fourth tooth that sticks up when their mouth is closed.
animals.blurb: Shy around people despite their size, American crocodiles prefer salty coastal waters and mangrove swamps over freshwater swamps.
animals.mapCaption: Coastal waters of Florida, the Caribbean and Central America

animals.name: Chinese Alligator
animals.funFact: One of the smallest crocodilians in the world, a Chinese alligator digs burrows deep enough to sleep through the whole winter.
animals.blurb: Fewer than 150 Chinese alligators remain in the wild, making them one of the rarest reptiles on Earth — though thousands live safely in breeding centers.
animals.mapCaption: Wetlands of the lower Yangtze River, eastern China

animals.name: Spectacled Caiman
animals.funFact: The bony ridge between a spectacled caiman's eyes looks just like a pair of glasses — that's exactly how it got its name!
animals.blurb: The most common crocodilian in the Americas, spectacled caimans often bask in large groups along riverbanks at dawn.
animals.mapCaption: Rivers and wetlands of Central and South America

animals.name: African Dwarf Crocodile
animals.funFact: The smallest crocodile species alive, a dwarf crocodile is armored with extra-thick bony plates, even on its belly.
animals.blurb: Dwarf crocodiles are shy and mostly nocturnal, spending their days hidden in burrows deep in the rainforest swamp.
animals.mapCaption: Swamp forests of West and Central Africa

animals.name: Mugger Crocodile

quickFacts.speed: Up to 20 mph (32 km/h) in short bursts

animals.funFact: Mugger crocodiles are champion diggers, digging long burrows to escape both blazing heat and dry seasons.
animals.blurb: Broad-snouted and adaptable, mugger crocodiles can survive in everything from rivers to city park lakes across South Asia.
animals.mapCaption: Lakes and rivers of the Indian subcontinent

animals.name: Black Caiman
animals.funFact: The largest predator in the Amazon, a black caiman can grow nearly as long as a school bus.
animals.blurb: Black caimans hunt mostly at night, using pits along their jaw to sense the tiniest ripples made by prey in pitch-black water.
animals.mapCaption: Rivers and flooded forests of the Amazon Basin
